description: Hospital's group-purchasing-organization (non-340B) acquisition cost for one levonorgestrel-releasing IUD device
source: UNVERIFIED. Only source found for this $537-$600 range is a single MDedge ObGyn article (mdedge.com/obgyn/article/103902), which every direct-access attempt failed: WebFetch returned truncated/no content twice, curl with a browser user-agent returned only a JS/cookie-consent shell (page requires client-side rendering and appears authwall-gated), archive.org is blocked for this tool, and the site's beta subdomain is not publicly routable (ECONNREFUSED). The Physicians' Alliance of America 'Liletta Pricing Update' bulletin, checked directly 2026-09-10, does not itself state these dollar figures -- it is a members-only order bulletin that only notes AbbVie's 2026 WAC increased, with pricing behind a login.

This range should be treated as unconfirmed until a hospital pharmacy buyer's actual GPO contract/invoice, a paid pricing database (Medi-Span, RedBook), or a readable copy of the MDedge article is obtained. Base value is still the midpoint of the unconfirmed $537-$600 range for lack of anything better; do not cite this parameter as verified in any downstream write-up.

description: Hospital's 340B-program acquisition cost for one Liletta levonorgestrel IUD, for a 340B-eligible (safety-net/disproportionate-share) hospital
source: AAFCPAs, 'LILETTA IUD May Offer Cost Savings to 340B Covered Entities' (2016-09-12), citing a Medicines360 pricing announcement. Independently corroborated by a second, undated source describing Liletta's '340B federal pricing' as $50 (checked 2026-09-10), though that source also does not resolve whether the price was later raised to $100.
notes: STALE PRICE WARNING remains: both sources found describe the $50 price without a current (2026) date, and neither confirms or denies the reported later increase to $100. Two independently-worded sources agreeing on $50 is modestly reassuring but is not the same as a current price list. Needs direct verification against Medicines360's current price list before use. Relevant because the hospital in this model's real MRF extract (Denver Health) is a safety-net/DSH hospital and is plausibly, but not confirmedly, 340B-eligible.

description: Denver Health's own published self-pay/discounted-cash price for HCPCS J7297 (levonorgestrel IUD, 52mg, 8yr), from its CMS-mandated price-transparency machine-readable file
source: Denver Health and Hospital Authority standard-charges MRF, downloaded directly 2026-09-10 from https://sthpiprd.blob.core.windows.net/machine-readable-files/7840/841343242_denver-health-and-hospital-authority_standardcharges.csv (file dated 2026-04-30); gross charge $2,393.32, discounted-cash $837.67, inpatient negotiated-equivalent $820.91
notes: Directly verified, single-institution primary source -- not a national estimate. Provided as a cross-check ceiling, NOT the base-case acquisition cost: chargemaster/cash prices include hospital margin above true acquisition cost, which is exactly why iud_device_acquisition_cost_gpo and _340b (far lower) are used for the actual cost-minimization base case.

description: Incremental operating-room minutes for IUD insertion performed at the time of bariatric surgery
source: General (non-bariatric-specific) IUD-under-anesthesia literature: Children's Hospital Colorado / CU Anschutz adolescent-gynecology 'IUD Placement Under Anesthesia' patient-care protocol, stating the insertion itself takes 5-15 minutes.
notes: No published study of IUD insertion added-time specifically during bariatric surgery was found despite multiple targeted literature searches (2026-09-10). This is a general-population proxy, exactly analogous to how the sibling Lynch-syndrome model used non-Lynch-specific literature for its office-EMB failure-rate parameter. Revisit if a bariatric-specific timed study is ever published.

description: Scenario toggle: is IUD insertion at time of bariatric surgery billed as a separate professional fee (e.g. a different proceduralist, modifier -59/XU), or bundled/not separately billable because it is a minor procedure added to an already-open case?
source: Model-owner structural assumption, not yet confirmed against a specific payer's bundling policy or a real claim. Default FALSE (bundled/no separate fee) is the more conservative assumption for the combined arm's cost advantage, since it means the combined arm's professional-fee savings are as large as possible.

description: Medicare (CMS) negotiated-equivalent inpatient rate for MS-DRG 621, 'O.R. Procedures for Obesity without CC/MCC' -- the host procedure, for context only
source: Denver Health and Hospital Authority standard-charges MRF, downloaded 2026-09-10 (same file as above), payer_name = CMS, plan_name = Medicare

Provided only so a reader can see the host procedure's scale relative to the IUD costs above.

description: 12-month probability of levonorgestrel-IUD expulsion when placed as a standalone office procedure (not combined with another surgery)
source: Masten E, et al. Body Mass Index and Levonorgestrel Device Expulsion in Adolescents and Young Adults. J Pediatr Adolesc Gynecol 2024;37:407-411. Retrospective chart review, single children's hospital, 588 nulliparous patients aged 10-19 with a 52mg LNG-IUD placed 2017-2021, 43 (16.2%) placed as a combination case with metabolic/bariatric surgery (MBS).
notes: This is the paper's reported 'overall' 12-month expulsion rate (5.6%), used here as a proxy for the non-combined/standalone rate since combined cases were only 16.2% of the cohort (the mixture effect on the overall rate is small). The paper's logistic regression reports an odds ratio (see iud_expulsion_odds_ratio_combined_vs_standalone) rather than a clean non-combined-only percentage, so this is an approximation, not a number read directly off a table. Population is adolescents/young adults, not the general bariatric-surgery population this model otherwise targets -- flagged as a general proxy, same caveat pattern as combined_arm_added_minutes.

description: 12-month probability of levonorgestrel-IUD expulsion when placed at the time of bariatric/metabolic surgery
source: Masten E, et al. Body Mass Index and Levonorgestrel Device Expulsion in Adolescents and Young Adults. J Pediatr Adolesc Gynecol 2024;37:407-411 (same paper/cohort as iud_expulsion_probability_standalone above).
notes: Directly reported figure (16.3% expulsion at 12 months in the combined-placement group, n=43), not derived/approximated. The paper's adjusted logistic regression found combined placement carried significantly higher expulsion odds than non-combined placement (OR=3.23, 95% CI not extracted here, P=.024) -- see iud_expulsion_odds_ratio_combined_vs_standalone for that figure directly. This is the single most important clinical-outcome finding differentiating the two strategies found in this project's literature review: it is a real cost/effectiveness tradeoff working AGAINST the combined arm's facility-cost advantage.

description: Adjusted odds ratio for 12-month IUD expulsion, combined bariatric-surgery placement vs. non-combined placement, from Masten et al. 2024's logistic regression
source: Masten E, et al. J Pediatr Adolesc Gynecol 2024;37:407-411, adjusted logistic regression, P=.024.
notes: NOT used directly in the cost engine -- provided as a cross-check on iud_expulsion_probability_standalone/_combined above: implied odds ratio from those two probabilities is (0.163/0.837)/(0.056/0.944) = 3.29, closely matching this paper-reported 3.23, which is reassuring internal consistency given _standalone was only approximated.

description: Probability that a standalone office IUD-insertion attempt fails outright and must be escalated to a sedated/procedure-suite re-attempt
source: Saito-Tom LY, Soon RA, Harris SC, Salcedo J, Kaneshiro BE. Levonorgestrel Intrauterine Device Use in Overweight and Obese Women. Hawaii J Med Public Health 2015. Retrospective cohort, 149 women (55 normal weight, 45 overweight, 49 obese). Obese group: 4% (2/49) failed insertion, 8% (4/49) 'difficult' insertion; no statistically significant difference by BMI group (P=.47).
notes: Chosen over an alternative source (Harrison, 'Failed IUD insertions in community practice,' Contraception 2012 -- 19.6% failure in nulliparous women choosing emergency contraception, inserted by nurse practitioners without adjuvant measures, at family-planning clinics) because Saito-Tom's obese-BMI-specific population is a much closer match to this project's target population than that emergency-contraception/nulliparous cohort, even though its sample is small (n=49, only 2 failures -- low/high bounds are 0%/8%, the observed failed/difficult rates, not a formal CI). On failure, this model assumes escalation to a sedated re-attempt costing the same added_or_cost as the combined arm's OR/anesthesia minutes, with no duplicate device or professional fee (see R/strategy_costs.R) -- a simplifying assumption, not a sourced escalation-cost figure.

description: Professional fee for routine IUD removal (CPT 58301), for context only
source: Denver Health and Hospital Authority standard-charges MRF, downloaded 2026-09-10 (same file as other Denver Health rows in this table); gross charge $607.35, discounted-cash $212.58.
notes: NOT used in the incremental-cost calculation. Every LNG-IUD is eventually removed (expiration, side effects, or patient choice) regardless of which strategy inserted it, so routine removal cost is common to both arms and cancels out under the incremental-cost principle, the same reasoning that excludes the base bariatric-surgery cost itself. Recorded explicitly here so the omission is a documented decision, not a silent gap.

description: Baseline uterine perforation risk per IUD insertion, general population, for context only
source: General LNG-IUD/copper-IUD perforation literature reviewed 2026-09-11: rates commonly cited as 0.3-2.6 per 1,000 insertions.
notes: NOT used to differentiate the two strategies. Evidence on whether anesthesia/sedation changes perforation risk is mixed and inconclusive: some sources suggest general anesthesia may modestly increase risk (excess force at the internal os without patient feedback), while a separately cited large study found no association between anesthesia use and perforation. Given no confident directional evidence, this model applies NO differential perforation-risk adjustment to either arm -- a documented decision, not an oversight. Revisit if a study specifically comparing office vs. sedated/OR insertion settings is found.

description: Average patient opportunity cost (time value at self-reported wage, plus travel time) per ambulatory medical visit -- applies to the standalone arm's dedicated office visit only; the combined arm requires no separate visit
source: Reused directly from the sibling emb_colonoscopy project: Ray KN, Chari AV, Engberg J, Bertolet M, Mehrotra A. Opportunity costs of ambulatory medical care in the United States. Am J Manag Care 2015;21(8):567-574 (PMID 26295356).
notes: Same verification limitations as in the sibling project (dollar_year inferred, not directly confirmed from primary text -- see that project's docs/data_sources.md). Inflated to reference_dollar_year using the general (all-items) CPI, data/cpi_all_items.csv, not the medical-care CPI, since a wage/time-based cost should track general price/wage inflation. This is a SOCIETAL-perspective add-on, reported alongside the healthcare-sector total, not folded into it, matching the sibling project's own healthcare-sector-vs-societal separation.

description: Independent commercial-insurance-claims benchmark for a 52mg levonorgestrel IUD's device + physician insertion cost, for cross-validation against the GPO/chargemaster figures above
source: Nguyen ABT, et al. Descriptive study of the real-world, long-term cost estimates and duration of use for hormonal and nonhormonal intrauterine devices using US commercial insurance claims. J Manag Care Spec Pharm 2023;29(12):1303-1311. IBM MarketScan commercial claims, 63,386 IUD insertions in 2014, 5-year follow-up.
notes: A THIRD independent cost channel alongside the Denver Health chargemaster ($837.67 cash price for J7297) and the unverified GPO estimate ($537-$600): this is what a commercial payer actually paid nationally for the combined device+insertion claim in 2014 dollars ($1,107 +/- $4). Not directly comparable to either other figure without adjustment (different year, and 'paid claim' sits between chargemaster and true acquisition cost conceptually), but useful triangulation. The same paper reports 5-year cumulative cost of $1,514 for the 52mg product, driven mostly by AUB/ovarian-cyst workup and removal/reinsertion, not modeled in this project. NOT used in the base-case cost engine.
